title: Terms
short: A term is a word or phrase that names a class or an individual; singular terms name one thing, general terms name a class.
trouble: Learners count words instead of ideas. "Large brown dogs" is one general term, and "the first president of the United States" is one singular term.

blocks.html: In The Three Acts of the Mind you met the term as the product of simple apprehension. A term is a word or phrase that names a class of things or one individual thing. In a proposition, terms are the building blocks that the verb joins.

A singular term names exactly one thing ("Mount Everest", "the tallest student in our class"). A general term names a class, so it applies to each of its members ("mountains", "students who play the violin"). Count ideas, not words.

Logic cares about what a phrase picks out, not how long it is. "The first president of the United States" uses seven words, but it names one person, so it works exactly like a name. "Dogs" is one word, but it applies to millions of animals. When we later ask whether a statement is about all of a class or only some of it, we need to know which phrases name classes.

blocks.title: Counting the terms in a proposition
blocks.q: How many terms does "The first president of the United States was a skilled surveyor" join, and what are they?
steps: Find what the sentence is about: "the first president of the United States". That whole phrase is one idea, a singular term.
Find what is said about it: "a skilled surveyor". That is a second term (a general term: there were many skilled surveyors).
blocks.a: 2 terms: "the first president of the United States" and "a skilled surveyor"

blocks.html: Counting words instead of ideas. "Large brown dogs" is one general term, not three, and "the first president of the United States" is one singular term. Check: could you replace the whole phrase with a single name or a single plural noun without changing what it picks out? Then it is one term.
